The failure rate is the same in the first and the last run (12.5%).
findings.fix: Nothing to fix; this is what the tool read. A clean report means none of the checks found anything in these runs, not that the tests are good.

findings.history: run-1 passed, run-2 flaky, run-3 passed, run-4 passed
findings.message: shop.checkout.PaymentTest > authorisesCard is flaky: the same test, on the same code, both passed and failed. It failed and then passed within one run (run-2): the report holds the failed attempts as flakyFailure or flakyError, which Surefire writes when a retry passes.
findings.fix: Treat it as a failing test, not a passing one: find the cause (state shared between tests, waits and timing, test order, the clock, a remote service), fix it, or move it out of the main suite until it is fixed. A retry hides the problem; it does not fix it.

basis.text: A test is non-deterministic when it passes sometimes and fails sometimes, without any noticeable change in the code, tests, or environment.
Then this test will be counted as a flaky test.
basis.section: Output flaky re-run information on the screen

findings.history: run-1 passed, run-2 passed, run-3 error, run-4 passed
findings.message: shop.checkout.PaymentTest > capturesPayment passed in 3 runs (run-1, run-2 and run-4) and failed in 1 run (run-3). The runs that disagree are of different commits (a1f3c9e, b7d2e40 and c5e8a13), so a code change may explain it.
findings.fix: Give the commit of each run with --commit, so that runs of one commit that disagree are reported as flaky. If the code did not change between these runs, rerun the test on one commit to confirm, then treat it as flaky.

basis.text: A test is non-deterministic when it passes sometimes and fails sometimes, without any noticeable change in the code, tests, or environment.
Such tests fail, then you re-run them and they pass.

findings.history: run-1 failed, run-2 failed, run-3 failed, run-4 failed
findings.message: shop.checkout.CartTest > appliesDiscountCode failed every time it ran: in all 4 runs. The last message: "expected total 45.00 but was 50.00".
findings.fix: Fix the code or the test, or delete the test if it no longer checks anything that matters. A test that always fails teaches people to ignore a red build.

basis.text: When a regression test goes red, you know you've got an immediate problem, often because a bug has crept into the system without you realizing.
basis.section: Why non-deterministic tests are a problem

basis.text: Once you start ignoring a regression test failure, then that test is useless and you might as well throw it away.
basis.section: Why non-deterministic tests are a problem

findings.message: shop.checkout.PaymentTest > refundsOrder takes 14.4 s at the median of 4 runs, above the limit of 10 s; the slowest was 15.1 s in run-3.
findings.fix: Find where the time goes: sleeps and fixed waits, real network or database calls, large fixtures, or one test that checks too much. Split it, fake the slow part, or move it to a slower suite on purpose. Raise --slow if this time is expected.

findings.message: shop.checkout.PaymentTest > sendsReceiptEmail took 3.4 s in run-4, 3.9 times its median of 0.875 s across 4 runs; the limit is 2 times.
findings.fix: Compare that run with the others: a slower service, a wait that ran to its timeout, a retry inside the test, or a change in the code under test. A test that is much slower in one run is often close to a timeout.

findings.history: run-1 skipped, run-2 skipped, run-3 skipped, run-4 skipped
findings.message: shop.checkout.CartTest > calculatesShippingForRemoteArea was skipped in all 4 runs. A test that is always skipped checks nothing, and it is easy to forget.
findings.fix: Run it again or delete it. A skipped test checks nothing; if it waits on a known problem, say which one in the skip message and review it on a fixed schedule.

basis.text: A danger here is that tests keep getting thrown into quarantine and forgotten, which means your bug detection system is eroding.
<xs:element name="skipped" nillable="true" minOccurs="0" maxOccurs="1">

findings.message: shop.checkout.CartTest > addsItemToCart appears 2 times in run-3, with the result passed each time. Two tests share a class name and a name, or a tool wrote every retry; tests with the same name cannot be told apart across runs.
findings.fix: Give each test a name that is unique within its class or suite. If the copies are retries that all ended the same way, there is nothing to fix.

findings.history: run-1 passed, run-2 passed, run-3 passed, run-4 passed
findings.message: shop.checkout.CartTest > keepsCartAfterLogin passed with a time of 0 and wrote no output in all 4 runs where it appears. That can mean a test that checks nothing, or one that is simply fast; the result file cannot tell them apart.
findings.fix: Open the test and check that it asserts something. If it does, there is nothing to fix; fast tests often report a time of 0.
